definition.title: Transit-oriented density
definition.handbook_text: Model the effect of increasing allowable residential density near major transit stops through higher building heights and/or increased floor area ratios. Teams should define major transit stops and justify their transit proximity threshold. Teams may assume that parking requirements are reduced or eliminated.
definition.description: More height and floor area near major transit stops (a rail station, or a bus stop with frequent weekday service; distances in the Model and Assumptions Overview), with reduced parking.

source.citation: Housing Data and Technology Innovation Challenge, Participant Handbook, "Benchmark Policy Scenarios" and "The five scenarios"

notes: Transit-specific ledger entries are added when this scenario is built.

parameters.label: First calendar year counted
parameters.rationale: Reforms are assumed to take effect on January 1, 2027, so the five years counted are 2027-2031.
parameters.revisit: Change only if the assumed effective date changes.

parameters.label: Years in the projection horizon

source.citation: Housing Data and Technology Innovation Challenge, Participant Handbook, "Benchmark Policy Scenarios" and "The five scenarios"

parameters.rationale: The Handbook asks every team to assume a five-year horizon.
parameters.revisit: Only if the Handbook changes.

parameters.label: Number of assumptions named in the "what would narrow the range" research agenda
parameters.rationale: The agenda names the few assumptions whose first-order share of the output's variance is largest. Three keeps it short enough to act on.
parameters.revisit: Revisit if a reform has more than three inputs of similar weight.

parameters.label: Homes added (state, five years) for the first "chance of adding at least" readout
parameters.rationale: A reform that clears this bar does something visible in at least a few places; below it the gain is lost in the noise of statewide permit counts.
parameters.revisit: Revisit with the spread of reform results once all five reforms are final.

parameters.label: Homes added (state, five years) for the second "chance of adding at least" readout
parameters.rationale: About two hundred homes a year statewide: a gain a state housing agency would notice in its annual permit totals.
parameters.revisit: Revisit with the spread of reform results once all five reforms are final.

parameters.label: Homes added (state, five years) for the third "chance of adding at least" readout
parameters.rationale: About one thousand homes a year statewide: a gain of the size the largest benchmark reforms reach in their middle estimates.
parameters.revisit: Revisit with the spread of reform results once all five reforms are final.

parameters.label: Homes added (state, five years) for the fourth "chance of adding at least" readout
parameters.rationale: About two thousand homes a year statewide: a gain that would change a state's housing outlook, a high bar for any single reform.
parameters.revisit: Revisit with the spread of reform results once all five reforms are final.

parameters.label: Width ratio (added homes to baseline) under which the effect is called "much less" uncertain than the level
parameters.rationale: When the likely range (P90 minus P10) of a reform's added homes is under a quarter of the width of the baseline's likely range, the sentence says the reform's effect is "much less" uncertain than the future level of building; under one it says "less"; otherwise it says the two are about as uncertain.
parameters.revisit: Revisit if readers misread the sentence in user testing.

parameters.label: Homes added in a tract (middle estimate) where the second tract-column class starts
parameters.rationale: Below one home over five years a tract's gain is in the first class, "under one home": the reform reaches the tract, but barely. Each break is five times the one before, so the classes stay readable from a single ADU to a block of apartments.
parameters.revisit: Revisit with the statewide distribution of tract gains once the map is in use.

parameters.label: Homes added in a tract (middle estimate) where the third tract-column class starts
parameters.rationale: About one home a year in one tract. Most tracts gain between one and five homes under a single reform, so this break marks the tracts that gain clearly more.
parameters.revisit: Revisit with the statewide distribution of tract gains once the map is in use.

parameters.label: Homes added in a tract (middle estimate) where the top tract-column class starts
parameters.rationale: About five homes a year in one tract: a gain a neighbourhood would notice, mostly near major transit stops or in large tracts with many single-family lots.
parameters.revisit: Revisit with the statewide distribution of tract gains once the map is in use.

parameters.label: Capitalisation rate used to value a finished mid-rise building
parameters.rationale: Larger, newer apartment buildings trade at somewhat lower cap rates than small ones.
parameters.revisit: Source from a published cap-rate survey for Pennsylvania metros.

parameters.label: Developer profit required on a mid-rise project, as a share of total cost
parameters.rationale: Developers and their investors typically need 10-20% on cost for larger projects.
parameters.revisit: Source from published feasibility studies.

parameters.label: Construction cost per square foot, mid-rise apartment building
parameters.rationale: Wood or light-steel frame over a concrete podium costs more per square foot than small buildings; the range covers region and finish.
parameters.revisit: Look for a free public construction cost source.

parameters.label: Operating costs as a share of rent, mid-rise apartment building
parameters.rationale: Vacancy, management, upkeep, insurance and property tax for a professionally run building.
parameters.revisit: Build from parts as for ADUs.

parameters.label: Soft costs as a share of construction, mid-rise apartment building
parameters.rationale: Design, permits, financing and other soft costs (other than the benchmark fee).
parameters.revisit: Source from published development pro formas.

parameters.label: Floor area per mid-rise apartment
parameters.rationale: New mid-rise apartments are mostly studios to two-bedrooms averaging about 850 sq ft.
parameters.revisit: Check against new multifamily construction characteristics (Census SOC).

parameters.label: Units in a typical mid-rise apartment project
parameters.rationale: Four- to six-storey buildings near transit stops typically hold a few dozen to about 150 apartments.
parameters.revisit: Check against permits for 5+ unit buildings in Pennsylvania metros.

parameters.label: Cost of one space in an above-ground parking structure

source.citation: UCLA Institute of Transportation Studies (February 2026), "No Such Thing as Free Parking", construction cost per space from 2025 Rider Levett Bucknall cost data for 17 U.S. cities, excluding land

parameters.rationale: Above-ground structures averaged about $52,000 per space across 17 cities, from $29,000 (Phoenix, Washington DC) to $99,000 (Portland), excluding land.
parameters.revisit: Check whether Philadelphia or Pittsburgh is among the 17 cities and use its value.

parameters.label: Cost of one surface parking space, land and construction

source.citation: Victoria Transport Policy Institute, Transportation Cost and Benefit Analysis II, chapter 5.4 "Parking Costs" (version of 3 October 2022), Table 5.4.4-1

parameters.rationale: The review's summary table puts surface parking land and construction at about $8,000 per space in 2022 dollars. Low covers cheap rural land; high covers urban land.
parameters.revisit: Update the price year to 2026 and check against a Pennsylvania cost estimate.

parameters.label: Cost of one underground parking space

source.citation: UCLA Institute of Transportation Studies (February 2026), "No Such Thing as Free Parking", construction cost per space from 2025 Rider Levett Bucknall cost data for 17 U.S. cities, excluding land

parameters.rationale: Underground parking averaged about $73,000 per space across 17 cities, from $40,000 (Washington DC) to $111,000 (Portland), excluding land.
parameters.revisit: Check whether Philadelphia or Pittsburgh is among the 17 cities and use its value.

parameters.label: Share of spaces in above-ground structures, transit-rich tracts
parameters.rationale: Where land is dear, more parking is stacked in structures; the rest is surface or underground.
parameters.revisit: Estimate from local project data or land prices.

parameters.label: Share of spaces underground, transit-rich tracts
parameters.rationale: Underground parking is mostly limited to large projects in the densest places.
parameters.revisit: Estimate from local project data or land prices.

parameters.label: Parking spaces required per apartment under current rules
parameters.rationale: Common local minimums for apartments are one to two spaces per unit.
parameters.revisit: Replace with a sample of Pennsylvania zoning codes.

parameters.label: Share of formerly required spaces still built, transit-rich tracts
parameters.rationale: After minimums are removed, projects near frequent transit still build about 60% of the spaces once required, because lenders and buyers still want parking.
parameters.revisit: Cite the post-reform studies of what developers built.

parameters.label: Extra units a small site can hold when parking is not required
parameters.rationale: Land no longer needed for parking can hold more homes on tight sites. The gain is small on average and zero where land is plentiful.
parameters.revisit: Test with the pro forma on typical lot sizes; cite site-yield studies.

parameters.label: Weekday departures that make a bus stop a major transit stop
parameters.rationale: The benchmark rule: a major transit stop is a fixed-guideway station, or a bus stop with at least 64 weekday departures (about every 15 minutes over 16 hours).
parameters.revisit: Only if the major-transit-stop rule changes.

parameters.label: Distance around a frequent bus stop counted as near transit
parameters.rationale: The benchmark rule: a quarter mile, straight line, for frequent bus stops.
parameters.revisit: Only if the major-transit-stop rule changes.

parameters.label: Stop-name likeness that can stand in for the reverse place check
parameters.rationale: When the reverse share fails (for example a schedule feed that also covers a neighbouring area), a pairing by place still holds if at least half the map feed's stops have a schedule stop within 50 m whose name is at least 0.8 alike (difflib ratio, lower case, punctuation removed). Renumbered stops usually keep their names.
parameters.revisit: With the place-paired feeds of each state build.

parameters.label: Share of a schedule feed's in-state stops that must sit at the map feed's stops to pair by place
parameters.rationale: A map feed whose stop ids match no schedule feed may be paired by place. Besides a shared distinctive agency-name word and half the map feed's stops within 50 m of the schedule's stops, half the schedule feed's own stops inside the state must lie within 50 m of the map feed's stops. A big agency's feed fails this against a small operator (an airport or a town shuttle) whose few stops sit at its stops.
parameters.revisit: After each state build, read the transit_feeds rows with paired_by = place.

parameters.label: Distance around a rail station counted as near transit
parameters.rationale: The benchmark rule: half a mile, straight line, for fixed-guideway stations.
parameters.revisit: Only if the major-transit-stop rule changes (the interface offers 1/4, 1/2 and 3/4 mile).

parameters.label: Equal-count bins used to estimate each input's share of the output's variance
parameters.rationale: The draws are sorted by one input and cut into this many bins with the same number of draws each. Ten bins of two hundred draws each keep the variance inside every bin well measured while still following a curved link.
parameters.revisit: Revisit if the number of draws changes a lot.

parameters.label: Medium-run supply response to a change in profit per unit

source.citation: Albert Saiz (2010), "The Geographic Determinants of Housing Supply", Quarterly Journal of Economics 125(3), 1253-1296, Table VI (metro areas with population over 500,000)
Nathaniel Baum-Snow and Lu Han (2024), "The Microgeography of Housing Supply", Journal of Political Economy 132(6), 1897-1946, abstract

parameters.rationale: Percent change in permitted units for a 1% change in the value-to-cost margin. Published metropolitan housing-supply elasticities for older northeastern metros mostly sit between about 0.5 and 2; 1.0 is a neutral central value until the cross-check job is run.
parameters.revisit: Cite the metro elasticity study and the 2024 tract-level study after reading them; cross-check with the planned elasticity cross-check (literature values against a long-difference estimate from permits and prices).

parameters.label: Share of a cost saving that reaches the decision to build
parameters.rationale: Part of any cut in fees or parking cost is captured by landowners as higher land prices rather than turning into more homes. Half is a neutral start; the range is wide because the evidence on who bears fees is mixed.
parameters.revisit: Read the evidence on fee incidence and narrow the range.

parameters.label: Most extra 5+ unit permits a county can absorb, as a share of its baseline 5+ unit permits

source.citation: Evidence library entry ev.tod.chicago_freemark: Yonah Freemark (2020), "Upzoning Chicago", Urban Affairs Review 56(3), abstract

parameters.rationale: New apartments must be rented: lenders and builders pace projects to regional demand, so a zoning change near stations moves only part of a county's apartment pipeline in five years. A county with no recent 5+ unit permits gets no TOD units.
parameters.revisit: Calibrate on station-area upzonings: added 5+ permits against the region's pipeline.

parameters.label: Premium over current value a mid-rise builder pays to assemble a site
parameters.rationale: Assembling several lots means paying holdouts above market; upzoning also raises asking prices (Chicago station-area land prices rose after upzoning).
parameters.revisit: Calibrate on station-area land sales after upzoning.

parameters.label: Chance a site redeveloped under TOD would have been redeveloped at today's floor area anyway in 2027-2031
parameters.rationale: The homes today's rules allow on a site are in the baseline only if the site would have been redeveloped in the window anyway. The authorizations subtracted from the reform's on a redeveloped site are this chance x the apartments today's floor area allows there. Sites near stations do turn over, but most that pencil only at the upzoned height would not be rebuilt at today's height, so the chance is well below one.
parameters.revisit: Estimate from station-area permits on parcels before and after upzonings.

parameters.label: Floor area ratio allowed today near major stops (before the reform)
parameters.rationale: Most land near Pennsylvania stations is zoned for houses, rowhouses or low-rise commercial, roughly FAR 0.4-1.4. Only floor area above this counts as added by the reform; the rest was allowed already (and is in the baseline).
parameters.revisit: Read base-district FARs near stations from municipal zoning codes.

parameters.label: Share of land near a major stop that could be rebuilt as mid-rise, rural tracts
parameters.rationale: Few rural tracts are near a major stop, and little of that land suits mid-rise.
parameters.revisit: Measure soft-site shares from parcel data near PA stations.

parameters.label: Share of land near a major stop that could be rebuilt as mid-rise, suburban tracts
parameters.rationale: Suburban station areas mix parking lots and strip retail (good sites) with single-family streets that rarely assemble into mid-rise sites.
parameters.revisit: Measure soft-site shares from parcel data near PA stations.

parameters.label: Share of land near a major stop that could be rebuilt as mid-rise, urban tracts
parameters.rationale: Block land near a station also holds parks, schools, churches, recent or large buildings, historic districts and small lots that cannot be assembled. Only a minority of it is a realistic mid-rise site within a decade.
parameters.revisit: Measure soft-site shares from parcel data (assessed improvement-to-land ratio) near PA stations.

parameters.label: End of the morning peak window (hour, exclusive)
parameters.rationale: Morning peak window 7:00 to 9:00. Windows use whole hours, because departures are counted per hour.
parameters.revisit: Only if the peak window definition changes.

parameters.label: Start of the morning peak window (hour of the service day)
parameters.rationale: Morning peak window 7:00 to 9:00 (start inclusive, end exclusive): the two busiest commuting hours in most U.S. schedules.
parameters.revisit: Only if the peak window definition changes.

parameters.label: Longest average scheduled headway that makes a bus stop frequent, in both peaks
parameters.rationale: A bus stop is a major stop under the walkshed rule when buses leave the same platform (one side of the street) on average at least every 15 minutes in both weekday peak windows, all routes added. Fifteen minutes is the usual frequent-service line in transit planning and in state transit-density laws; the daily benchmark rule (64 departures) is its all-day cousin.
parameters.revisit: Test 10 and 20 minutes by rebuilding the table with an override; revisit if a Pennsylvania bill defines frequent service.

parameters.label: Heading difference beyond which a trip leaves a bus pole the other way
parameters.rationale: Peak departures are counted per platform-level stop with all routes added, because GTFS direction_id is defined route by route. A pole is split into two sides only when some trips leave it heading more than 120 degrees away from its main heading (the bearing to each trip's next stop; main heading = the 30-degree sector with the most trips). 120 rather than 90 degrees leaves room for routes that turn at the next corner, which are still on the same side of the street.
parameters.revisit: Check split poles by hand on a map in Philadelphia and Pittsburgh (loops and terminals).

parameters.label: End of the afternoon peak window (hour, exclusive)
parameters.rationale: Afternoon peak window 16:00 to 18:00.
parameters.revisit: Only if the peak window definition changes.

parameters.label: Start of the afternoon peak window (hour of the service day)
parameters.rationale: Afternoon peak window 16:00 to 18:00 (4 to 6 pm).
parameters.revisit: Only if the peak window definition changes.

parameters.label: Share of a mid-rise site the building covers
parameters.rationale: Mid-rise buildings cover most of the lot; setbacks, courtyards and access take the rest.
parameters.revisit: Check against recent mid-rise site plans in Pennsylvania.

parameters.label: Floor area ratio of the low-rise TOD prototype (variant)
parameters.rationale: Three to four storeys with surface parking cover less of the lot than a mid-rise with a garage. Used only by the variant 'tod_lowrise'.
parameters.revisit: Measure from site plans of recent walk-up apartment projects.

parameters.label: Construction cost per sq ft of the low-rise TOD prototype (variant)
parameters.rationale: A wood-frame walk-up has no elevator core, concrete podium or garage, so it costs less per square foot than the mid-rise (multifamily.hard_cost_per_sqft). Used only by the variant 'tod_lowrise'.
parameters.revisit: Price from published construction cost guides for garden and walk-up apartments.

parameters.label: Storeys of the low-rise TOD prototype (variant)
parameters.rationale: A three- to four-storey wood-frame walk-up with surface parking: the building small-town and rural station areas can support. Used only by the variant 'tod_lowrise'.
parameters.revisit: Check against recent walk-up apartment permits in Vermont and rural Pennsylvania.

parameters.label: Smallest number of existing homes per acre used to price a site
parameters.rationale: A site is priced as its existing homes x their value. Land near stations with few homes (shops, parking lots) still costs something; this floor prices it like a few houses per acre.
parameters.revisit: Replace with assessed land values near stations.

parameters.label: Share of a mid-rise building's floor area that is apartments
parameters.rationale: Corridors, stairs, lobbies and services take 12-25% of gross floor area.
parameters.revisit: Check against published mid-rise efficiency ratios.

parameters.label: Share of TOD units that are new to the region (not moved from elsewhere in it)
parameters.rationale: Some apartments built near stations would have been built elsewhere in the same region anyway; the reform only moves them. Those are not counted. The range is deliberately wide, and this is a headline caveat.
parameters.revisit: Estimate from regional 5+ unit permits before and after station-area upzonings.

parameters.label: Rent of a new mid-rise apartment as a multiple of the tract's two-bedroom median
parameters.rationale: New buildings with amenities near transit rent above the existing stock, most of which is decades old.
parameters.revisit: Compare new-lease asking rents with ACS medians near PA stations.

parameters.label: First-year mid-rise permits as a share of the full yearly rate
parameters.rationale: Mid-rise projects take one to three years from site control to a building permit.
parameters.revisit: Check against permit timing after station-area upzonings.

parameters.label: Years for mid-rise permits to reach the full yearly rate
parameters.rationale: Larger projects need assembly, design, financing and approvals; slower than ADUs.
parameters.revisit: Check against permit timing after station-area upzonings.

parameters.label: Share of feasible mid-rise sites permitted each year

source.citation: Evidence library entry ev.tod.chicago_freemark: Yonah Freemark (2020), "Upzoning Chicago", Urban Affairs Review 56(3), abstract

parameters.rationale: Station-area upzonings are taken up slowly: Chicago's found no detectable rise in permits within about five years, while land prices rose. A few percent of feasible sites a year keeps five-year take-up well below capacity.
parameters.revisit: Calibrate on station-area upzonings with permit counts (Minneapolis, Seattle, Chicago full paper).

parameters.label: Two-bedroom rent as a multiple of median gross rent, where the two-bedroom median is blank
parameters.rationale: In Pennsylvania tracts the two-bedroom median is close to the all-units median gross rent.
parameters.revisit: Compute from ACS B25031 tracts that report both.

parameters.label: Years after January 1, 2027 before mid-rise permits near stops start to respond
parameters.rationale: The benchmark reform is assumed to be in force on the first day of the window; the one-to-three-year path from site control to a permit is in the ramp (tod.ramp_first_year_share).
parameters.revisit: Set from a bill's effective date when a bill is modelled.

parameters.label: Share of a state by-right multi-family district's land that lies inside the TOD walk distance
parameters.rationale: Massachusetts already zones districts for multi-family homes by right near transit (MBTA Communities, Section 3A). Upzoning that land again adds no new mid-rise sites, so the TOD reform takes it out. A district counted as inside a station area can still reach past the half-mile circle, so only this share of its acres is taken out, never more than the tract's land near a stop. Read only by variant tod_ma_acre_share (and by a pack that has a district table but no 3A capacity table). Since M1b the benchmark compares the 3A parcels' own modeled capacity (mbta_3a_capacity_tract) with the prototype on the same land instead.
parameters.revisit: Replaced in the benchmark by the 3A capacity comparison; kept for the variant bridge.

parameters.label: Share of a state's bus stops with measured service needed to show a statewide TOD range
parameters.rationale: Bus stops whose scheduled departures were not counted (no readable feed) have unknown service, and nothing bounds what they would add. When at least half of the National Transit Map's bus stops in a state were measured, the measured part is the larger part and the statewide range is shown with a "partial footprint" label. Below half, the unknown part is the larger part: the statewide range and percent change are suppressed and only the measured contribution is reported, labelled. Rail stops count as measured (major by mode). A rule for display, not sampled.
parameters.revisit: If a bound for unmeasured agencies (for example from published route headways) becomes available.

parameters.label: Floor area ratio allowed near major stops after the reform

source.citation: Evidence library entry ev.tod.california_sb79_2025: California Senate Bill 79 (2025), state floors of 80-120 homes per acre and 55-75 ft near stops

parameters.rationale: The reform's definition, not an uncertain number. FAR 2.5 with 850 sq ft apartments and 82% net floor area is about 105 homes per acre, inside California SB 79's 80-120 per acre floors. Change it to study a stronger or weaker upzoning; 0 (or anything at or below today's allowed FAR) adds nothing.
parameters.revisit: Revisit if a Pennsylvania transit-density bill sets its own floors.

parameters.label: Storeys allowed near major stops after the reform

source.citation: Evidence library entry ev.tod.california_sb79_2025: California Senate Bill 79 (2025), height floors of 55, 65 and 75 ft

parameters.rationale: The reform's definition. Five storeys (about 55-65 ft) is the common wood-over- podium mid-rise. The usable floor area ratio is the lower of the FAR limit and storeys x lot coverage.
parameters.revisit: Revisit with a Pennsylvania bill text.

parameters.label: Width counted on each side of a reached street or path
parameters.rationale: Land counts as reached when it lies within 50 m of a street or path that is within the walking distance: about one lot depth (typical Pennsylvania lots are 30 to 60 m deep). Wider buffers fill large blocks; narrower ones leave block interiors out.
parameters.revisit: Compare with parcel depths near stations once parcel data cover more counties.

parameters.label: Smallest network piece a stop may join
parameters.rationale: A stop whose nearest network nodes belong to a connected piece shorter than one mile (1,609 m) in total is on a fragment (a platform or a path the map does not link to streets). The network is treated as incomplete there and the stop uses its straight-line circle, flagged as fallback.
parameters.revisit: Check fallback stops by hand; lower it if complete small towns are being flagged.

parameters.label: Farthest a stop may be from the walking network to join it
parameters.rationale: A stop joins every walkable network node within 80 m, starting at its straight-line distance. Stops sit on streets or platforms, so 80 m is ample; a larger value would let walks jump across rail cuts and highways.
parameters.revisit: Check the stops that fall back to straight lines by hand.

variants.name: tod_network_half_mile
variants.title: TOD within a 1/2-mile walk (peak frequent-bus rule)
variants.question: What if major stops are rail plus buses every 15 minutes in both weekday peaks, and land counts within a 1/2-mile walk on the street network?

variants.name: tod_network_quarter_mile
variants.title: TOD within a 1/4-mile walk (peak frequent-bus rule)
variants.question: How much smaller is the effect if only land within a 1/4-mile walk counts?

variants.name: tod_network_three_quarter_mile
variants.title: TOD within a 3/4-mile walk (peak frequent-bus rule)
variants.question: How much larger is the effect if land within a 3/4-mile walk counts?

variants.name: tod_lowrise
variants.title: TOD with a 3-4 storey walk-up prototype
variants.question: Would a cheaper three- to four-storey walk-up with surface parking pencil where the mid-rise does not?

variants.name: tod_ma_acre_share
variants.title: TOD with the older acre-share rule for land already zoned by right (Massachusetts 3A)
variants.question: What did the TOD estimate say when a share of each 3A district's acres was taken out of the land that could become a mid-rise site, instead of counting only the capacity above what the district already allows?

variants.name: tod_capacity_screen
variants.title: TOD screened for practical capacity (sewer, flood zone, steep slope)
variants.question: How many of the station-area homes can be built in practice once land without public sewer, in the flood zone or on steep slopes is screened?
